Who bills a Knoxville house

Living within Knoxville means two tax bills a year. One office, the Knox County Property Assessor, decides the value both are built on. Collection is split: the City of Knoxville Revenue Office takes the city share, and the Knox County Trustee takes the county share. Do not mix them up, since the city says money sent to the wrong office leads to mistakes.

  • City bill: Revenue Office, 865-215-2084, Suite 453, City County Building, 400 Main Street; weekdays 8:00 to 4:30. Send mail to P.O. Box 15001, Knoxville, TN 37901-5001.
  • County bill: Trustee, 865-215-2305, Suite 427 in that building, same weekday hours. The mailing box is P.O. Box 70, Knoxville, TN 37901, and six Trustee locations accept payment.
  • Questions about a value: the Assessor at 865-215-2360.
  • Questions about a deed: the Register of Deeds at 865-215-2330.

Both sets of contacts appear on the city's property tax page, and the county's Trustee page covers the county side.

Knoxville housing in brief

Knoxville, the Knox County seat, had an estimated 202,021 residents on July 1, 2025, a 6.0% rise from 2020. Owners live in just 46.6% of homes, so renters are the majority, and a house for sale here may come with a tenant. A typical owner-occupied house is valued at $239,700, rent in the middle runs $1,191, and there are 86,263 households.

Older neighborhoods such as Fourth and Gill, Parkridge and Fort Sanders hold many Victorian and bungalow houses, Sequoyah Hills and Lindbergh Forest have 1920s and 1930s homes, and Bearden and Fountain City joined the city when it annexed them in 1962. The University of Tennessee's main campus keeps renters and buyers coming.

How the bill is figured

Step one is the appraisal. The assessor then applies a percentage that depends on how the property is used, and each taxing body multiplies the result by its own rate per $100. Percentages from the assessor's guide: residential and farm 25 percent; commercial and industrial 40 percent; business personal property 30 percent; public utilities 55 percent.

A two-year reappraisal cycle means values here are refreshed often. Between cycles the assessor picks up new construction and reviews a portion of the county annually. Any change to a value or classification requires an Assessment Change Notice. Rates are voted by the county commission and the city council; neither the assessor nor the city does any appraising of its own.

Budgets move the rates. For today's numbers, call the Revenue Office (city) and the Trustee (county), or look at the most recent bill.

Due dates and penalties

October 1 is the city due date, and March 1 of the next year is when the tax is delinquent. From then the city charges 1 percent penalty plus 1 percent interest every month. Early payers get a 1% discount on real estate tax if they pay by the end of October; for 2026 that window has closed, and it never covers personal property or public utility tax.

Payments go to the oldest unpaid year first, which means an old delinquent balance swallows money you meant for the current bill. County payments can be made in person, online at propertytax.knoxcountytn.gov, by mail, or by phone at 865-215-2305, option 3. Card payments carry a 2.5% vendor charge and e-checks $1.00; the city's online fees also go to its vendor rather than the city.

How to appeal your assessment

Call the assessor at 865-215-2360 for an informal conversation, and take the matter to the county equalization board if it goes nowhere. Three grounds are accepted: your value is too high, someone else's is too low, or your property is classed wrongly, for example commercial shown as residential. Complaining about the amount of tax does not work, because the assessor does not choose the rate.

The county board opens June 1, and a dispute that skips it generally becomes final. A loss there can go to the State Board of Equalization, filed by August 1 or within 45 days of the date on the county board's notice, whichever is later. An administrative judge hears the case and decides within 90 days after the hearing. Still unhappy? A chancery court petition must come within 60 days once the state board's order is final. The Comptroller's appeals page walks through each step. Miss the June window and you wait for the next notice cycle.

Tax relief and the senior freeze

The Trustee's relief page lists a state credit and a freeze. The credit pays part of the bill. It is not an exemption, so the full bill still arrives and the owner pays it.

  • Elderly and disabled homeowners can receive up to $85 for 2026, as long as combined 2025 income across all owners is at most $38,470.
  • Disabled-veteran owners and their widows or widowers can receive up to $444 with no income limit, if the owner's service-connected rating is permanent and total.
  • Senior freeze: owners who turn 65 by December 31, 2026 can lock the base tax on one home and up to five acres, if 2025 income, VA income included, stays under $63,470.

Apply again every year, by April 5. City tax relief questions go to the Revenue Office at 865-215-2084.

Selling with taxes owed

The tax follows the house no matter what the sales contract says. Even if the seller promised to pay, unpaid tax becomes the next owner's debt, and the city says private agreements do not limit its right to collect. Buyers can request the parcel's bill from the Revenue Office, and a seller with back tax should line up payoff numbers early from both the city and the Trustee.

Splitting the year's tax is up to the buyer and seller, and the title company normally does the math at closing. Sellers who carry a balance, a pending appeal or an inherited property can ask the title company where each item lands on the settlement statement.

Delinquent parcels can also end up in a Tennessee tax sale, where bidders must be current on their own taxes. Paying off an old balance before you list keeps your house out of that process. Sensible order of work: city payoff first, then county payoff, then a check of which years are still open, then everything to the title company.

Frequently asked questions

Does the City of Knoxville collect the same tax as Knox County?

No. They are separate taxes at separate rates. Houses within the city normally get a bill from the Revenue Office and another from the Trustee, each with its own phone number and payment address.

Is there a Knoxville city discount?

Only for real estate tax paid by the end of October, which earns 1% off. After that the full amount applies, and delinquency starts March 1 of the next year.

Who should I call if my Knoxville assessment looks too high?

Phone the Assessor at 865-215-2360 for an informal look. A chat is not an appeal, so protect your rights by filing with the county equalization board, which sits from June 1.

Will a buyer owe my unpaid Knoxville tax?

Yes, in the sense that the lien stays with the house. Because unpaid tax becomes the new owner's obligation despite any promise by the seller, a title company usually takes any balance out of your proceeds at closing.

How do I find out whether I qualify for relief on a Knoxville home?

Read the Trustee's relief page or call 865-215-2305. You need to own and live in the home, and income limits govern the elderly and disabled credit and the senior freeze. April 5 is the application cutoff.

Who sends the property tax bill in Nashville?

Two Metro offices split the work. The Assessor of Property decides what your house is worth for tax purposes, and the Office of the Metropolitan Trustee mails the bill and accepts payment.

Nashville and Davidson County operate as one Metropolitan Government, which is why the Trustee acts as the county's tax collector. On top of real property, the office collects personalty and public utility taxes, runs the state tax relief, tax deferral and tax freeze programs, and handles delinquent taxes, Central Business Improvement District taxes, Gulch district taxes and vegetation liens. The Assessor's office is at 700 President Ronald Reagan Way, Suite 210, Nashville, TN 37210.

  • Tax billing and collection, including payoff questions: 615-862-6330
  • Mortgage inquiries at the Trustee: 615-862-6330
  • Tax relief and tax freeze applications: 615-862-6140
  • Assessor call center for appeal appointments: 615-862-6059

How a Nashville bill is figured

Four pieces make up the math: appraised value, assessment ratio, assessed value and tax rate. The Assessor sets the appraised value. State law fixes the ratio at 25 percent for residential and farm property, 40 percent for commercial and industrial property and 30 percent for personalty.

The Metro Council sets the rate, and it is not final until the State Board of Equalization certifies it. The Trustee shows one rate for the Urban Services District and another for the General Services District, each stated per hundred dollars of assessed value. Your bill shows which district your parcel is in.

Metro Trustee tax rates by service district
Service districtRate per $100 of assessed value
Urban Services District$2.814
General Services District$2.782

To estimate a bill, multiply your appraisal by the ratio, divide by 100, then multiply by the rate for your district. Your appraisal notice and the Trustee's lookup give the real numbers.

When are Nashville property taxes due?

Statements go out in October, and tax must be paid in full by the last day of February to avoid interest. For the bill mailed in October 2026, that deadline is February 28, 2027.

Payment is accepted at the Trustee's office or at a First Horizon Bank financial center, which takes Metro property tax payments from October through February under an arrangement with the Trustee. If a lender escrows your taxes, the servicer normally pays the bill, but the Trustee's mortgage inquiry line can confirm whether a payment posted. Check that before you sign a sale contract, because a missed escrow payment turns into a closing item.

How to appeal your Nashville assessment

Begin with the Assessor and, if that fails, move to the independent Metropolitan Board of Equalization. Informal review closes in the spring, in April, and scheduling a formal appeal closes in late June, so watch the Assessor's site each spring for the exact dates.

The Board of Equalization is created under Metropolitan Charter Article 11, Chapter 2. It has five members appointed by the Mayor and confirmed by the Council, serving two-year terms, and it can send cases to hearing officers. It sits from the first business day of June until that year's equalization is finished. Book through the call center at 615-862-6059.

Bring evidence that supports a lower value as of January 1 of the appeal year:

  • Comparable sales close to your home in age, features and square footage, with size within about 20 percent of yours
  • Any fee appraisal you already hold, which the board treats as an opinion to review and not an automatic answer
  • Repair estimates for needed work, not routine upkeep
  • Photographs of damage or outdated kitchens and baths

A relative may file for the owner. Anyone else, including an attorney or tax representative, needs a signed letter of authorization that names the parcel and the assessment year. If the board's decision disappoints you, you have 45 days after the board mails its notice to go to the State Board of Equalization.

Tax relief for Nashville homeowners

Homeowners aged 65 and up, disabled homeowners, disabled veteran owners and surviving spouses of disabled veteran owners can apply for state-funded tax relief through the Trustee. The program dates to a 1973 constitutional amendment, and Metro adopted it locally.

For the current window the Trustee lists an income cap of $38,470 for Davidson County, measured on 2025 income for all owners and a spouse. Applicants must have turned 65 by December 31 of the tax year, show the home is their principal residence, and sign a form that lets the Trustee check income with the IRS, Social Security or the state. Applications run through April 5, 2027. Anyone already enrolled in the relief or freeze programs must return a voucher by April 5 every year to stay in. Call 615-862-6140 before you gather paperwork, because the veteran and spouse routes use separate forms.

What happens when Nashville property tax goes unpaid?

After the last day of February, the bill is delinquent and interest applies under Tennessee law. The Trustee's office handles delinquent taxes, so that is where you ask for a payoff figure with interest counted through a specific closing date.

Liens matter to a seller too. The Trustee collects vegetation liens and the special district taxes mentioned above, so ask whether any of them sit on your parcel. A title company will search for all of them. Pulling an account history from the Trustee early keeps a surprise charge from delaying closing.

Selling a Nashville house with tax still owed

You can sell it. Unpaid property tax is cleared from the sale money at closing, and the title company asks the Trustee for the exact amount.

  • Call 615-862-6330 and ask for the balance, interest and any lien lines on your parcel.
  • Tell the closing agent the date you expect to close so interest is counted to that day.
  • If the house is vacant or inherited, confirm who the Trustee has on file to receive the bill, since a statement mailed to a former owner is easy to miss.
  • Compare any offer with the amount owed, because a low price can leave you short of the tax and loan balances.

Owners facing a large tax balance often weigh a sale to a buyer who closes as-is, which saves repair costs and showing time. Whatever route you choose, get the payoff in writing from the Trustee before you accept terms.

Davidson County housing snapshot

Davidson County had 745,904 residents in the July 2025 estimate, a 4.2 percent rise over the 2020 base, with 389,379 housing units and 324,907 households for 2020 to 2024. Owners occupy 52.8 percent of homes, so close to half of households rent. The median owner-occupied value is $417,400 and median gross rent is $1,582.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a separate Nashville city tax on top of the county tax?

No. Nashville and Davidson County are one government, with one rate per service district: $2.814 in the Urban Services District and $2.782 in the General Services District, each per hundred dollars of assessed value. Your bill shows which applies to your parcel.

By what date must 2026 Nashville property tax be paid to avoid interest?

The last day of February 2027, which is February 28. The Trustee mails statements in October.

When can I appeal my Nashville property value?

Informal review with the Assessor closes in the spring, and scheduling a formal Board of Equalization appeal closes in late June. After a board hearing, the state board accepts an appeal for 45 days after the notice is mailed.

Who qualifies for Nashville property tax relief?

Owners aged 65 and up, disabled owners, disabled veteran owners and their surviving spouses, if they meet the income limit. The Trustee lists $38,470 for Davidson County based on 2025 income, and applications are open through April 5, 2027.

Who do I call to find out what I owe before closing?

Call the Metropolitan Trustee's tax billing and collection line at 615-862-6330 and ask for a payoff that includes interest to your expected closing date. Give the same figure to your title company so the balance comes out of your proceeds.

Who sends the property tax bills for a Chattanooga house?

A house inside the city limits gets billed by two governments, Hamilton County and the City of Chattanooga. The Hamilton County Assessor of Property sets the appraisal, the Hamilton County Trustee collects the county bill, and the City Treasurer collects the city bill.

The Trustee also collects for Collegedale, East Ridge, Lakesite, Red Bank, Ridgeside, Soddy Daisy and Walden, but not for Chattanooga. Paying the Trustee therefore never covers the city share.

  • Hamilton County Trustee: Room 210 of the Hamilton County Courthouse on Georgia Avenue, plus a satellite office at 6125 Preservation Drive, Suite 101. Doors are open weekdays from 8 to 4. Call (423) 209-7270.
  • City Treasurer: City Hall, 101 E. 11th Street, Room 100. Phone (423) 643-7262 or email ptax@chattanooga.gov.
  • Hamilton County Assessor of Property: (423) 209-7300, for values, mailing address changes and exemption requests.

Due dates and penalties

Notices are mailed in September, and the due date is October 1. Paying through the last day of February avoids interest. From March 1 it starts running.

Hamilton County adds 1.5 percent for every month of delay, which works out to 18 percent a year. Chattanooga divides the same charge into 1 percent interest and a half percent penalty. A mailed county payment is late if the post office does not postmark it in time, while an online payment counts on the day you make it.

A bill is for one calendar year, yet it lands late in that year, so a spring sale can leave the prior year's bill outstanding. New owners are told to read the closing statement to learn who covers it.

How the tax on a Chattanooga house is worked out

The county Assessor sets an appraised value, a state ratio turns that into an assessed value, and each government multiplies by its own rate per $100. Residential and farm land is assessed at 25 percent and commercial and industrial land at 40 percent. Reappraisal comes around every four years.

What happens if the tax goes unpaid?

Skipping the bill leads to court in roughly a year. Once taxes have sat open for twelve months past the due date, the city files them in Hamilton County Chancery Court, and overdue stormwater fees are sent to a collection agency at that moment.

After filing, payment moves to the Clerk and Master at 625 Georgia Avenue, Courthouse Room 300, phone (423) 209-6606. The city says a parcel can be sold for delinquent tax after three years. Hamilton County runs the tax sale every June and leaves the former owner one year to redeem.

A stormwater fee rides on the city bill, so any payoff should include it. Partial payments are applied in a fixed order: stormwater fee interest, then stormwater fee, then tax interest and penalty, then the tax itself.

How to pay or look up a bill

Find the parcel on the city's tax search page, or ask the Treasurer for a copy. A bill that never showed up does not move the deadline.

  • Online: card payments carry a 2.55 percent fee with a $2.20 minimum, and e-check carries $2.00. The city keeps none of it.
  • By mail: City Treasurer, P.O. Box 191, Chattanooga, TN 37401-0191. Send the original bill with its barcode between October and the end of February.
  • In person: City Hall, Room 100, all year. Full payments are also taken at First Horizon branches in Hamilton County when you bring the original bill.
  • County bill: the Trustee accepts partial payments, and its satellite office at Bonny Oaks handles tax relief appointments.

Tax relief for Chattanooga homeowners

Owners who are elderly, disabled or disabled-veteran households qualify for state-funded Tax Relief, and the city separately offers a Tax Freeze that holds the bill at the first amount you qualify at. A single Tax Relief form reaches both the city and the county.

For the 2026 year the city sets a $38,470 ceiling on combined 2025 income for the elderly and disabled groups, and age 65 or disability must be in place by December 31, 2026. The maximum reimbursement is $162.12 for those two groups and $844.38 for each disabled veteran owner or surviving spouse. The 2026 bill must be paid before the application can be processed, and applications close April 5, 2027.

United Way covers the stormwater fee on the city bill for anyone approved for either program. For help with the paperwork, call (423) 643-7274.

How do you appeal a Chattanooga property appraisal?

Phone the Assessor of Property at (423) 209-7300 before filing anything. When the call settles nothing, the county Board of Equalization is next, and going around that board generally closes the door on later appeals.

Expect the county board to open its session on June 1. The State Board sits above it and takes appeals filed by August 1 or within 45 days of the county board's notice, whichever comes last. Ask the Assessor what this year's window is before you plan around any date.

The Chattanooga housing market in brief

The city's population was 194,144 in July 2025, compared with 181,099 at the 2020 count. For 2020 to 2024 there were 79,084 households, owners reported a $283,200 median home value, and median rent was $1,256. Owners occupy just 52.4 percent of homes, so many sellers have tenants in place.

Selling a Chattanooga house with tax owed

Before closing, ask the title company to order a payoff for each open tax year, with the county, city and stormwater amounts broken out. The balance follows the property after transfer, since Hamilton County says unpaid taxes continue to accrue against it.

Overdue tax, interest and any court costs usually come out of the sale proceeds at the closing table. A bill already filed with the Clerk and Master needs that office's own payoff number, which will not match the Treasurer's. The deed is recorded at the Hamilton County Register of Deeds after the payoff, and the title company normally does both.

If you plan a quick cash sale, the same payoff work applies. Collect the three balances, confirm any relief application is paid up, and bring the original bills to the closing table.

When do Chattanooga property taxes become late?

Both bills go late on March 1, five months after the October 1 due date. After that, 1.5 percent is added to the unpaid amount each month.

Do I pay Chattanooga city tax and Hamilton County tax separately?

Yes. They are two bills with two collectors, the City Treasurer and the Hamilton County Trustee. Paying one leaves the other open.

Can I get help paying my Chattanooga property tax bill?

Yes, if you are elderly, disabled or a disabled veteran. The city takes state Tax Relief applications and also runs a Tax Freeze. Applications for 2026 close April 5, 2027, after the bill is paid. Call (423) 643-7274 with questions.

What if I never received a Chattanooga tax bill?

You still owe the tax and any interest, since a missing bill excuses nothing. Look up the parcel on the city's search page or phone the Treasurer at (423) 643-7262.

The county Trustee's office is at 157 Poplar Ave., with branch locations and a mailing address of P.O. Box 2751, Memphis, TN 38101-2751. Online and payit901 app payments are available. A $1.50 e-check fee or a 2.6% card fee applies, and the county keeps none of it.

The Trustee also runs ManagedPay, which spreads the current-year tax into monthly payments through February. Interest, legal fees and court action still attach to anything left unpaid after the deadline, so the plan fits an owner who is staying more than one about to close.

Tax relief and payment plans for older or disabled owners

Memphis owners can look at three programs, all governed by state eligibility rules.

  • Tax Relief: for owners 65 or older, or totally and permanently disabled and receiving Social Security disability, who meet income limits, and for qualifying 100% disabled veteran owners and their surviving spouses.
  • Tax Freeze: for owners 65 or older whose income stays under the limit the state sets each year.
  • Quarterly Payment Program: for owners 65 or older who live in their primary residence and owe nothing delinquent.

The quarterly program needs a new application every year. Call the Trustee at (901) 222-0200 to ask when the next window opens and to confirm you qualify. Relief works as a reimbursement of tax already paid, so the bill itself is still yours to pay.

Can you dispute a Shelby County value?

Yes, though the season is short. Shelby County's equalization board hears appeals from May 1 through June 30, a month earlier than the June 1 opening most Tennessee counties use. Miss it and you wait for next spring.

The board sits at 1075 Mullins Station Road, Suite C-142, Memphis, TN 38134, and you can call (901) 222-7300. There is no filing fee. You can file online while the season is open, mail the form, or hand it in at the counter. Expect to carry the burden of proof, since the assessor's number starts out presumed right. Bring comparable sales, an outside appraisal, photographs of defects and repair quotes.

A neighbor's lower bill is not a reason the board will accept, and it cannot waive penalties, adjust rates or rule on exemptions. A written decision arrives roughly two weeks after the hearing. Anyone still unhappy has 45 days from that notice to take the case to the State Board of Equalization, which hears Memphis cases locally.

A successful appeal produces a refund of any overpayment, and the Treasury says refunds generally take about 60 days after it receives the change. Keep paying on schedule in the meantime.

Selling a Memphis house with taxes owed

Memphis can put weed cutting, demolition and board-up, sidewalk work and anti-neglect charges on the same bill. A house with a code history may owe a good deal beyond the tax. Downtown properties may also carry Central Business Improvement District taxes.

Once taxes are a full year late, the account goes to delinquent tax attorneys on February 1 and legal costs get added. Clear things up before that stage if you plan to list.

  1. Ask the City Treasury and the county Trustee each for a payoff figure good through your expected closing date.
  2. Check the record for city charges that ride on the bill, not only the tax.
  3. Hand both figures to the title company so it can pay each balance from your proceeds on closing day.
  4. Afterward, update the owner name. The Trustee bills the owner on the Assessor's rolls as of January 1 and also draws ownership data from deeds recorded with the Register, so call 901-222-0200 once the change is on record.
  5. If the mailing address on the city bill is wrong, send the Treasury a signed written request after the Assessor's office has processed the change.

A cash sale that closes as-is skips repair work and showing time, but the same two payoffs still come out of the proceeds.

Frequently asked questions

When does Memphis city property tax become delinquent?

Once August 31 passes. Payment opens after the Council fixes the rate, typically around late June, and unpaid city balances then grow by 1.5% each month.

When is Shelby County property tax due?

Payment opens the first Monday of October and stays fee-free until February ends. Paying in October earns no discount.

Can I pay Memphis property tax in installments?

Owners 65 or older who live in the home and carry no delinquent balance can. The city splits the bill into four equal installments due August 31, November 30, February 28 and May 31. The Trustee sets its own terms, so ring (901) 222-0200.

How do I appeal my Shelby County property value?

Send it to the county equalization board between May 1 and June 30. Nothing is charged to file, and (901) 222-7300 reaches staff who can help with the forms.

Does a Memphis house with unpaid tax have to be sold at auction?

Not by default. A real estate account a full year behind is handed to attorneys on February 1 with legal costs added, but settling it from your closing proceeds clears the debt before that point.

Chancery Court orders the sale for cash. New owners are directed to the closing statement to see who pays for the year of transfer. Whatever is unpaid remains on the property itself. A closing agent can request payoffs from the Trustee and the city and settle both out of the sale proceeds.

Ask for a calculation of the share of the calendar year each side owns the house. The county Assessor posts a proration calculator that splits the year at a date you choose, which gives you a starting number to compare with the closing statement.

Yes, two bills mean two payments. The Trustee handles the county portion and the city handles its own portion for any house inside Clarksville.

A parcel two or more years delinquent can be put up at the Montgomery County tax sale. The owner then gets a one year redemption period.

The Montgomery County Assessor of Property answers at (931) 648-5709. A formal appeal is heard by the county Board of Equalization, usually starting June 1. Ask the Assessor for the filing cutoff.

The city applies its own rate to the county's assessed value. The county mails the bills and the city collects its portion. The city's property tax page lays out the process.

Before you list, gather the parcel number from your last notice and a copy of the most recent bill from each collector. Those two papers let the staff pull up your account quickly and give the title company something concrete to work from.

The Murfreesboro market and what it means for taxes

Murfreesboro is the seat of Rutherford County, about 34 miles southeast of downtown Nashville in Middle Tennessee. The 2020 census counted 152,769 people, and the July 2025 estimate is 171,178, an increase of 12.0%. The median owner-occupied home is worth $402,100, compared with $382,600 for the county, and owners live in 52.4% of homes. Median household income is $80,108 and median gross rent is $1,481.

At a median value above $400,000, the tax is a meaningful line on a settlement statement. Know the exact amount owed before you set a price, and remember that a buyer's lender will look at the bill when sizing the monthly payment. A tidy tax record, with nothing delinquent, makes a listing easier to close.

What the 2026 reappraisal means for your bill

Tennessee requires a countywide reappraisal every four years, and Rutherford County's last cycle before this one was 2022. Between cycles, values hold steady except for new construction, additions, demolition or corrections.

A higher appraisal does not automatically raise the tax. Under the state's certified tax rate law, a city or county must hold public hearings before it adopts a rate that collects more in total than the year before. The County Commission sets the rate, not the Assessor. A lender's appraisal can also differ from the Assessor's figure, since a lender studies one house in more depth than a mass appraisal can.

The math is simple. Take the appraised value and multiply by 25 percent for residential property, 30 percent for business personal property or 40 percent for commercial. Divide by 100, then multiply by the rate. The county rate was $1.8762 per $100 for 2025. Because 2026 was a reappraisal year, ask the Trustee or the city for the rate on your current bill and do not reuse an old figure.

Tennessee offers relief to homeowners 65 and over, to disabled homeowners, and to disabled veteran owners and their surviving spouses. Find the Revenue Office at the west end of City Hall's ground floor, with weekday hours of 8:30 to 4:30 and closures on national holidays. City business licenses also come from the Revenue Office, so an owner renting out a Jackson house should ask whether one is required. The City Recorder holds ordinances, resolutions and any deeds the city owns, and the public can request to look at them.

Residential property in Jackson is taxed on 25% of appraised value. Multiply that assessment by the City of Jackson rate plus the Madison County rate and you have the bill. The county's online estimate tool applies the percentages in this table.

How to appeal your assessment

First, call the Assessor and have the property record checked. If the value still looks wrong, take it to the Madison County Board of Equalization, a five-member panel of local property owners. Hearings run on weekdays during the first two weeks of June, and appointments can be booked in the final two weeks of May.

You can contest only this year's value; 2025 taxes, for instance, are closed to challenge in 2026. If the county board rules against you, the next stop is the State Board of Equalization. File by August 1, or within forty-five days of the date on the county notice if that is later. The state charges a fee of $10 to $17, partly nonrefundable. Keep paying the undisputed portion on time so the account does not go delinquent mid-case.

A state property tax freeze program is also listed by the county. Relief pays you back after the bill is settled, so every bill must still be paid, and only a primary residence qualifies. Ask the Trustee at (731) 423-6027 when applications open.

Online city payments handle real property, meaning land and buildings, as well as personal property, meaning business equipment. A typical homeowner owes only the real property bill, found by searching a parcel ID or street address.

Once the sale closes, the buyer should have the Assessor change the mailing address, since both billing offices take addresses from that record. Missing your parcel ID? The city's payment guide explains how to search by street address in the public records tool.

A workable sequence for sellers: find the parcel ID, check whether the house is inside city limits, request a written payoff from each billing office, and give both to the closing agent. Do this early, because the Revenue Office and the Trustee keep different hours and each has its own phone line. Anything owed is subtracted from your proceeds at the table. In a cash sale the same payoffs apply, but there is no lender waiting on a long approval, so the tax figures are often the last piece the closing agent needs. Jackson at a glance

As the Madison County seat, Jackson lies 70 miles east of Memphis and 130 miles southwest of Nashville. It had 69,339 residents in 2025, compared with 68,205 in 2020, and 27,541 households. Other Sullivan County payment rules:

  • A courtesy notice is mailed, though Tennessee does not require one
  • Installments are allowed between October 1 and February 28, and you track the balance yourself
  • Cards carry a 2.5% fee and e-checks a $1.25 fee
  • Interest runs at 1.5% per month from March 1, and payment is taken through March 15 before the account moves to the Clerk and Master

Kingsport and Sullivan County rates

Kingsport's 2025 city rate is $1.67 per $100 of assessed value, down from $1.99 for 2024. Sullivan County's 2025 rate is $1.6129. The city links the drop to the state's two-year ratio appraisal, which cost Kingsport about $3.8 million a year in revenue, and to Sullivan County's 2025 reassessment, its first since 2021. Residential property is assessed at 25% of appraised value, and your bill uses your own rates and assessment, so check the notice you receive.

Kingsport housing in brief

Kingsport lies along the Holston River in western Sullivan County and reaches into Hawkins County. Kingsport City Schools serve almost every resident, with Dobyns-Bennett High School as the main high school. The city had 57,530 residents on July 1, 2025, up 3.6% from April 2020, and 25,021 households. About 60.1% of homes are owner-occupied, the median owner-occupied home value is $234,100, median gross rent is $907, and median household income is $52,490.

Because a fair share of households rent, a seller may be handling a rental with tenants. Check both city and county balances early so nothing surprises the closing agent.

A short checklist before listing: confirm the city balance at 423-343-9860, confirm the county balance with the Trustee, note whether any part of the lot lies in Hawkins County, and keep your last notice handy. Title companies ask for those first, and having them ready shortens the closing. If a payoff request goes out well before the closing day, ask for an updated figure the week of closing so the penalty and interest line up with the actual date.

Disputing a higher value

Values follow a set yearly cycle. Ownership and condition are fixed as of January 1, change notices are due by May 20, and the county board of equalization meets starting June 1 and through that month. Sullivan County reassessed in 2025, so many Kingsport owners saw a new number that year. Check the notice in May each year for the same reason.

Steps if you disagree with a value:

  • Call the Sullivan County Assessor before the June board meets and ask whether an informal review is offered
  • File with the county board of equalization, since skipping it generally ends later appeal rights
  • Gather sales of similar Kingsport houses and explain differences in age, condition and size
  • Pay the undisputed part of the bill on time while the dispute is open

The state's appeal rules start at the county board, and the Sullivan Assessor can tell you when it sits.

Relief for seniors and disabled owners

The city has a relief program for elderly or disabled homeowners within income limits, and it links a brochure and the state Comptroller's relief page. Sullivan County has no Tax Freeze program, so relief is the route here. If you have a mortgage, the relief voucher must be signed and returned by April 5 each year or the state voids the credit.

Relief pays back part of what you owe after the fact, so keep paying the bill on time while an application is pending. Ask City Hall or the Trustee for the paperwork well before April. A seller who plans to list in the spring should check whether a voucher is pending, because an unsigned voucher can cost a credit that would otherwise reduce the bill.

Selling with unpaid tax

The owner of record on January 1 receives the notice, and a buyer who closes later is still responsible for seeing that the tax is paid on time. The settlement statement spells out the split. Once the November 30 city deadline passes, city penalties and county interest keep growing each month, so ask for payoff figures dated close to the closing day.

Unpaid tax is cleared from the seller's proceeds at the table. Call the city at 423-343-9860 and the Trustee in Blountville for written payoffs. A cash buyer can close on a short timeline and take on the paperwork, which helps if a house has fallen behind or sits in an estate.

Frequently asked questions

What happens if I miss the November 30 Kingsport deadline?

A 2% penalty applies on December 1, another 2% on January 1, and 1% each month after until you pay. Mail, the night deposit box and the City Hall counter at 415 Broad Street are all accepted.

Is the Kingsport city rate going up or down?

The 2025 city rate is $1.67 per $100, lower than the $1.99 charged for 2024. The city ties the shift to the state's ratio appraisal and the 2025 Sullivan County reassessment.

Where do I pay the Sullivan County part of my Kingsport tax?

Pay the Sullivan County Trustee in Blountville or at the Kingsport satellite office on West Center Street, open Monday through Wednesday from October 1 to March 15. Online and phone payments add card or e-check fees.

Does Kingsport have a tax freeze for seniors?

Sullivan County has no Tax Freeze program. The state tax relief program covers eligible elderly and disabled owners, and the voucher goes back by April 5.

Can a Kingsport house with unpaid taxes still be sold?

Yes. Unpaid city and county balances are paid from the seller's proceeds at closing. Get written payoff figures from the city and the county Trustee before the closing date.

Who sends the property tax bill in Collierville?

A Collierville house is taxed by two bodies: the Town of Collierville and Shelby County. The town's tax department answers questions at 901-457-2281 or propertytax@colliervilletn.gov, and residents owe county tax in addition to the town's.

On the county side, the Assessor of Property establishes value, the Board of Commissioners picks the county rate, and the Trustee prints the notices and mails them to whatever address the Assessor holds. If a lender escrows your taxes, the servicer may request the figures and pay the bill, but the Trustee still advises borrowers to keep the original notice.

Because the notice follows the Assessor's mailing address, anyone who has moved should update it well before October.

How a Collierville tax bill is figured

The town rate is $1.62 for each $100 of assessed value. Tennessee assesses homes at 25% of appraisal, so the town bill is a quarter of the appraised value times that rate, divided by 100.

Other classes use different percentages: 40% for commercial and industrial parcels, 55% for public utilities, 25% for farms and 30% for personal property. Add the Shelby County rate on top, which the Trustee or the Assessor can quote for your parcel. With a median owner-occupied value of $485,900, a typical Collierville assessment is large even before the county share is added.

Due dates and delinquency

County bills can be paid from the first Monday of October, and no interest builds before the end of February.

Collierville is in the group whose bills turn delinquent March 1. Unpaid base tax then gains 1.5% a month, which the Trustee states as 18% a year. Mail a check with the stub from your notice to the Shelby County Trustee, P.O. Box 2751, Memphis, TN 38101-2751, and make sure the postmark is no later than the last day of February.

Call Trustee customer service at (901) 222-0200 with account questions. Tenn. Code Ann. 67-5-2405 requires the Trustee to sue for delinquent real estate tax. The parcel carries a tax lien until the whole balance is cleared.

How to appeal your Collierville assessment

Evidence that points to market value carries the most weight with the Assessor. For a Collierville house, these help:

  • A private appraisal done recently.
  • Interior and exterior photographs showing condition.
  • For income property, three years of income and expense records.

Read the purchase contract and settlement statement to see who covers the current year's tax.

If you are behind, interest piles up each month from March 1 and a lien stays on the parcel until you clear the balance. Calling the town and the Trustee for a payoff is the right first move.

A cash sale does not change any of this. The title company still needs two payoff letters, and the settlement statement should show the town and county amounts on separate lines. Having them early keeps the closing date from slipping.

A year of Collierville property tax, month by month

Knowing the calendar helps a seller decide when to list and what to expect at closing.

  • End of February: last day to pay without interest. A mailed check needs a postmark by then.
  • March 1: unpaid base tax becomes delinquent and starts gaining 1.5% a month.

A house that closes in the middle of this calendar still has a tax bill attached to it, which is why the settlement statement matters so much.

What to have ready for the title company

A little preparation shortens the payoff process. Before you accept an offer, collect the following.

  • The latest town notice and the latest Shelby County notice, with the original stubs if you still have them.
  • Proof of the address the Assessor holds for you, since notices follow it.
  • Your lender's escrow statement, if a servicer pays the taxes from an escrow account.
  • Any paperwork from a value dispute, including the date of an informal review or county board hearing.

The title company will ask the Trustee at (901) 222-0200 and the town at 901-457-2281 for payoff figures. A surprise balance at either office should be settled before the contract date. The lien does not go away until everything owed is paid.

The town rate is $1.62 for each $100 of assessed value, applied at the state's 25% residential ratio. Shelby County bills its own rate on top, and the Trustee or the Assessor can tell you what it is for your parcel.

Unpaid base tax accrues 1.5% a month starting March 1, which is 18% a year. The Shelby County Trustee uses the same rate for Collierville, Arlington, Lakeland, Millington, Memphis and the county itself.

No. A review is a chance to pass along information so values match the market, and many disputes end there. An actual appeal is filed with the Shelby County Board of Equalization, typically by the last working day of June.

Who bills property tax inside Columbia city limits?

City property tax due dates

Columbia accepts city payments without penalty from November 1 through December 15. The City Recorder handles real and personal property under the same window.

Late charges stack up in three steps after the window closes:

  • A 0.5% charge applies through the end of December.
  • Another 0.5% accrues starting January 1.
  • From February 1, the city adds 1% for every month the balance stays open.

How and when do you pay Maury County tax?

The county calendar is longer than the city's. Payment opens in early October and stays penalty-free until the final day of February. Interest of 1.5% starts on March 1 and climbs monthly.

Partial payments are welcome, though interest applies to anything unpaid on March 1. A postmark counts as the payment date until the Trustee hands delinquent accounts to Chancery Court on April 1.

The Trustee offers several ways to pay:

  • Mail a check to Maury County Trustee at the same address.
  • Use the drop box outside the office after hours, with checks only.
  • Pay online by card or e-check; the vendor, not the county, takes a 2.5% fee.

An owner who thinks the value is unfair can go to the local board of equalization, then to the State Board. Help comes in two layers. A state program covers seniors, owners who are completely and permanently disabled, and disabled veteran owners with their surviving spouses. On top of that, the city gives a modest credit of up to $75 a year to qualifying seniors.

How to estimate a Columbia tax bill by hand

The Assessor's method is appraised value times the ratio for the property class, then that product times the rate. A home in Tennessee's residential class uses 25%.

Divide the assessed value by 100, then multiply by the county rate and by the city rate. Get both from the Trustee and the City Recorder, since the Maury County Commission and the city council set them through their budgets.

In a reappraisal year the appraisal itself moves, so set the new notice beside last year's before you assume the total will look the same.

Selling a Columbia house with taxes open

Show a buyer the tax history up front. Request written balances from the Trustee and the City Recorder before listing. A county balance still open at April 1 goes to Chancery Court, so settle it before that date. Payments postmarked on time are honored up to then.

At closing, the title company usually collects both balances from the sale proceeds. Two collectors and two calendars make a Columbia closing a little more involved than a county-only sale. A simple order of work keeps it tidy.

  3. Check whether a relief or senior credit application is pending, since those are due January 20.
  4. Give both figures to the title company so each appears on the settlement statement.
  5. Settle any county balance before April 1, when delinquent accounts move to court.

Because county notices follow the January 1 owner, the seller's name may still sit on a bill that arrives after closing. Forward it to the title company so the proration is handled in writing.
